doc.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017

chapter: Old styles, big bands and rhythm sections
title: Swing-era feel: drummers, bassists and rhythm guitar
summary: They discuss how swing drummers felt time, Remo Palmier's dislike of four to the bar, Pizzarelli on Basie, and Benny Carter and Kenny Washington.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Yeah. I have an internal debate sometimes when you’re playing them and the tenor player stands up to solo and is playing like they’re in the Tower of Power. And well —
Yeah. I’m with you on that man. It’s like, “Come on, man, come on.”
It’s almost better that they don’t know that it doesn’t fit. Because if they know it doesn’t fit then I think they’re making a bad musical decision.

But it’s almost like if you take them to task then you also have to sort of take the drummer to task. Because chances are the drummers in those bands weren’t keeping time on the hi hat, they were probably using the bass drum more. And it’s a whole different feel actually. I don’t think anybody today really knows how those drummers felt time. The bop thing has taken over. So everybody plays like a bop drummer now, even the swing guys. So that’s just the way it is. Even the bass players are pushing more than they did in those days. I think it’s like the same kind of feel. I should say they’re more laid © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

back now. I think they pushed more in those days. They were more in your face. And of course you could hardly find any guitarists that wanted to just play rhythm. They just don’t want to do that. In fact I had a guitar teacher, Remo Palmier, who said to me, “I don’t do that four to the bar nonsense.”

Yeah. He didn’t think that was cool. That’s old fashioned. That’s from another time. So when he would play in a big band he wouldn’t do the four to the bar. He just did sort of like comping and that kind of thing, if he played with them at all.

Bucky Pizzarelli said something that made a lot of sense to me. I asked him about, especially the early Basie band why they were so good. He said, “Well the drummer, and the rhythm section but especially the drummer didn’t try to hit every kick the horns were playing.”
Because if you do then you don’t have the back and forth. And after he said that I said well yes, of course.

So if you get in front of a high school band and they have those drum parts that are so – there’s way too much in them, and the poor drummers are trying to hit everything and you just take the music away.

Yeah. That happened in a Benny Carter session actually with Kenny Washington playing drums. And he was trying to do that, get all the hits. And I think at some point Benny Carter got frustrated with him and said, “Don’t bother with all that nonsense, just play the drums. Just play the drums. Just lay out a rhythm. That’s all I need.” It’s interesting stuff.
